correctness.rationale: For a fixed environment, changing one trial from ℓ to h raises the strict majority probability by (h−ℓ) times the central r-success mass of the other 2r trials, and the reverse change in the other state subtracts the corresponding mass. The central masses A and P in RESULT.md are related by bit complementation and interchanging h and ℓ at every position. Each paired likelihood ratio is Q^(k−r), independent of the number of successes in the first block. As a separate coefficient replay, let λ=(1−h)(1−ℓ)/(hℓ). The factor 1−h+hz is [h/(1−ℓ)] z (1−ℓ+ℓλ/z), with the analogous swapped identity. Taking the middle coefficient of the product of 2r factors gives ratio [h/(1−ℓ)]^k [ℓ/(1−h)]^(2r−k) λ^r=Q^(k−r). All these masses are strictly positive for the stated interior rates. Since ℓ(1−ℓ)−h(1−h)=(h−ℓ)(h+ℓ−1), the exact increment has the sign of h+ℓ−1 on k<r. Reflection ties r and r+1 and gives all other maximizing sets and strict comparisons. When h+ℓ=1 the states complement all the bits, so for odd size the success probabilities sum to one. The proof replays from RESULT.md lines 34–66 and is valid for every allowed integer and real rate. The exact-rational convolution checker was inspected, not executed; its finite grid is supplementary. No extension to even cohorts, changed quorum, unequal environmental weights, imperfect mirroring or long-term fitness is inferred.

value.rationale: The strict majority is a motivated nonlinear finite-cohort objective, for which individual marginal rates alone do not distinguish allocations. The theorem makes a sharp all-size decision between the opposite extremes of composition and gives the exact gap on each step. That is more informative than a numerical toy example or a mean-survival conclusion; the value is a probability-model boundary, not an ecological prescription or long-run bet-hedging conclusion.
